1.pericope_label: In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet
debates: Whether this is the Zechariah slain between the temple and the altar
Why the prophet is called son of Iddo in one place and son of Berechiah in another
Whether the call to turn implies a fresh backsliding
outliers: Henry reads the dating by a foreign reign as itself a confession of what sin had cost them
Clarke argues from the summons that no man is lost for want of power to return
Keil and Delitzsch settles the prophet name against two older renderings, as he whom God remembers
themes: Two prophets set to confirm each other
A grandson stepping into an office his father did not live to hold
A tomb pointed out and a claim nobody can check
Privileges that aggravate guilt where there is no holiness

4.pericope_label: Be ye not as your fathers, unto whom the former prophets have cried, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye now from your evil ways
debates: Whether both questions are the prophet or the second is the people answer
Whether the passage means prophecy is ending or that prophecy came true
Whether the word means take hold of or overtake
outliers: Ellicott turns the second question into an objection from the audience, which changes the whole argument
Ellicott reports an early rabbinic reading and rejects a rival that would make the passage about prophecy dying out
Wesley infers from the narrative that the prophet paused and let them frame their own answer
themes: Ancestors quoted as a warning rather than a precedent
Prophets who did not sin and died all the same
Words that overtake a man like a pursuer
A confession put into the mouths of the dead

7.pericope_label: Upon the four and twentieth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Sebat, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah
debates: Whether the night is a symbol or only a date
Whether the rider is the angel of the Lord or Christ before his incarnation
Whether the myrtles and the colours carry particular meanings at all
outliers: Ellicott denies that the night is symbolic and says the vision was seen awake, not in a dream
Ellicott argues from the Hebrew construction that the man among the myrtles and the angel of the Lord are one
Ellicott catalogues the symbolic readings of others as specimens rather than adopting any
themes: A shady hollow that hides what is in it
A sermon answered three months later by a vision
Horses ranked behind their captain
A colour that is neither all dark nor all light

9.pericope_label: Then said I, O my lord, what are these? And the angel that talked with me said unto me, I will shew thee what these be
debates: Whether the interpreting angel is distinct from the rider or is Christ himself
Whether the rest of the earth is good news or the problem
Whether the word answered implies a question at all
outliers: Ellicott reads the world at rest as self-confident security, set against a promise of shaking made two months earlier
Gill notes that the rider takes the answer out of the interpreting angel mouth, and calls it an honour done to the prophet
Ellicott insists the word means the whole earth, not the land, as the same word often does elsewhere
themes: A guide assigned to explain what is seen
Scouts sent out and reporting back
Nations quiet while one people is not
A calm that makes the question urgent rather than answering it

12.pericope_label: Then the angel of the LORD answered and said, O LORD of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah
debates: From what point the seventy years are counted
Whether God was little displeased in degree or only for a little while
Whether the verb rendered spread abroad carries its usual bad sense
outliers: Clarke and Ellicott both reject the obvious reckoning of the seventy years and then disagree on the replacement
Ellicott presses the perfect tense of the verb, making the jealousy already shewn rather than newly begun
Ellicott prefers helped for evil, so that the nations wished not to chastise but to annihilate
themes: A plea that asks only how long
An answer given to the interpreter rather than the asker
Instruments who exceeded their commission
A measuring line stretched over a ruin

18.pericope_label: Then lifted I up mine eyes, and saw, and behold four horns. And I said unto the angel that talked with me, What be these?
debates: Whether the four horns are the four great empires
Whether the workmen are carpenters, smiths, or watchers
Who the four workmen stand for
outliers: Ellicott dates the vision by a tense, arguing that a perfect in the dependent clause forbids reading the scattering as future
Clarke reports a correspondent who traces the word for workman back to silent attention and would render it watchers
Gill prefers blacksmiths to carpenters, on the ground that the horns to be cut off were iron
themes: Bulls tossing what they are enraged at
Four points of the compass, each with an enemy on it
A ploughman heed that keeps a furrow straight
Instruments raised against instruments
